US HIGH-YIELD BOND WEEKLY WRAP
June 26, 2025
Chasing the sun
Despite geopolitical headwinds, the high-yield bond market remains 
resilient, with weekly issuance expected to top $9 billion. June is 
on pace to exceed $32 billion in issuance — the highest monthly 
volume in nine months. Meanwhile, high-grade dealmaking topped 
expectations, with $32 billion priced in just four days (June 23-26), 
pushing June’s total to $96 billion.	
— Commentary, page 4
While the outlook isn’t any clearer now than it was on “Liberation 
Day,” high-yield borrowers pressed the pace in the second quarter, 
taking advantage of a remarkable full recovery in prices and spreads 
after early April market seizures.	
— US High-Yield Quarterly Wrap, page 5

High-yield primary: Unfazed	
	
       page 4
Despite rising geopolitical tensions, the high-yield bond market 
has remained largely steady. Primary issuance this week is 
expected to top $9 billion, slightly up from last week’s $8.93 
billion. The number of tranches also rose, with 12 expected to 
price by Friday, versus 10 last week. June is on track to surpass 
$32 billion in issuance by this week’s close, marking the highest 
monthly volume in nine months.
High-yield secondary: Chasing the sun

Cash-bond prices advanced over the week and the new-issue 
pipeline churned as a roiling geopolitical backdrop failed to 
diminish risk appetite. Treasury rates eased further off their 
June peaks, while spreads edged five basis points tighter from 
Monday’s open, to 293 bps off the curve. Meanwhile, the 
option-adjusted spread on LCD’s flow-name sample of liquid 
high-yield issues tightened 19 bps this week, to T+282.

US HIGH-YIELD BOND WEEKLY WRAP
June 26, 2025
Despite rising geopolitical tensions, the 
high-yield bond market has remained 
largely steady. Primary issuance this 
week is expected to top $9 billion, 
slightly up from last week’s $8.93 
billion.  
The number of tranches also rose, with 
12 expected to price by Friday, versus 
10 last week. June is on track to surpass 
$32 billion in issuance by this week’s 
close, marking the highest monthly 
volume in nine months and the largest 
June total since 2021, when it reached 
$39.53 billion.
While 2025’s volume continues to trail 
2024, the gap has started to narrow. Pro 
forma year-to-date volume of $140.18 
billion through June 27 is down 13% 
from the same period last year.
High-yield performance has provided a 
glimpse into the appetite for risk assets. 
The average spread to US Treasuries 
tightened two basis points in the week 
to June 25, to T+293, according to the 
S&P US Issued High Yield Corporate 
Bond Index. The average yield to worst 
shed 26 bps to 7.14%. June’s 1.36% 
return includes a 0.70% weekly gain, 
for a year-to-date return of 4.08%, 
the index shows. The riskiest segment 
of the index — CCC bonds — led the 
gains with a 1.04% seven-day return. 
Double-B paper returned 0.62%, and 
single-B notes 0.69%.
While refinancing remains the 
primary driver of issuance, several 
deals this week supported leveraged 
buyouts and M&A. 
High-yield primary market: Unfazed
Sizzling Platter, which owns the Little 
Caesars, Jamba, Wingstop, Dunkin’ 
and Jersey Mike’s brands, approached 
investors with a $500 million secured 
notes (B/B3) deal in connection with 
Bain Capital’s buyout of the company. 
The seven-year paper cleared at par 
to yield 9.50%, or at the tight end of 
guidance. 
The company also landed a $425 
million term loan B and an $80 million 
delayed-draw term loan to finance 
the transaction. Proceeds will repay 
existing debt and back general liquidity.
StoneX added to the M&A allotment via 
its $625 million placement for seven-
year secured bonds (BB-/Ba3). The 
company pitched the deal to investors 
to support its planned acquisition of 
R.J. O’Brien. The tranche priced at par 
to yield 6.875%, following guidance 
floated in the 7% area. The company 
will also use cash on hand to fund the 
$900 million purchase. Earlier in June, 
it entered into a restated $650 million 
senior secured revolver due June 2028, 
which upsized the facility from $500 
million and pushed out the maturity 
from the previous April 2026 due date.
Skechers USA, via a bond package to 
fund its LBO by 3G Capital, also added 
to the recent ramp-up in cross-border 
bond issuance. After removing dollar-
denominated seven-year secured notes 
from the offering, the fixed-rate debt 
was placed as €1 billion of seven-year 
(non-call three-year) senior secured 
notes (BB-/Ba3/BB-) at 5.25%, and 
$2.2 billion of 10% cash/10.75% PIK 
eight-year senior PIK toggle bonds (B+/
Caa1/B-). The euros priced at the tight 
end of 5.25% talk, and the PIK bonds 
priced in line with guidance and with a 
$300 million downsize. The financing 
package also includes a $1.55 billion 
seven-year term loan, a €1.25 billion 
seven-year term loan, and $4.4 billion 
in common equity. Skechers has also 
entered into a $1.6 billion revolver as 
part of the financing, according to a 
bond investor presentation.
Maxam Prill and Czechoslovak Group 
also successfully completed cross-
border bond deals.
— Jakema Lewis

US HIGH-YIELD BOND WEEKLY WRAP
June 26, 2025
High-yield borrowers swoop on rapid recovery in eye of tariff storm
While the outlook isn’t any clearer now than it was on 
“Liberation Day,” high-yield borrowers pressed the pace 
in the second quarter, taking advantage of a remarkable 
full recovery in prices and spreads after early April market 
seizures. After a sluggish $8.6 billion output in April, May’s 
$31 billion of issuance was followed by $14 billion over the 
first 17 days this month, making it the busiest June since 2021, 
when borrowing costs plumbed record lows.
Per Morningstar indices, HY has returned about 2.5% in Q2 
and 3.5% YTD, with those other categories all within striking 
distance. (Investment-grade bonds were up 0.6% for the 
quarter and 3% for the year.)
Making up for lost time
That weak April issuance total — about a third of last year’s 
output and the lowest for the month since 2008 — reflected 
pricings during just five sessions all month. (The primary 
went quiet between the April 2 “Liberation Day” tariff 
announcement and April 15.) 
That’s just 24% of the available sessions.
But, as prices gained and investors reeled in slack spreads 
after the April shocks, that utilization surged to 57% of May’s 
business days, and it was 67% from June 1-17, per LCD.
See this story and the underlying Excel data on the 
PitchBook platform.

Monthly HY issuance volume ($B) and secondary pricing
For a time, it wasn’t clear when the markets would recover 
from “Liberation Day,” which sparked the biggest single-week 
withdrawal from high-yield funds on record and sent broad-
market spreads soaring. (At the highs, spreads were about 
150 bps wide of the YTD low in February.)
But bellwether HY bonds (as measured by LCD’s running flow-
name bond sample) staged a furious comeback. The average 
bid level plunged more than three percentage points in the 
days after the April 2 tariff announcement, nearing 90% of 
par. By June, it had recovered that and more, topping 94% for 
three straight weeks to June 18. Its spread level, at T+409 on 
April 10, was down to T+268 by mid-June.
HY retail funds — which suffered outflows of more than $13 
billion across three weeks post April 20 — have recovered all 
but $1 billion of that over eight straight inflows to June 18.
That’s as high-yield maintained a slim lead over leveraged 
loans, investment-grade bonds and Treasuries through the Q2 
return swings.

Refi retreats; M&A/LBO and recaps stir
Part of the lull is in opportunistic refinancings. Issuers had 
printed more than $45 billion of bonds to this point last year 
to take out institutional and pro rata loans, a high since 2021. 
The tally is less than half that this year ($22 billion).
That’s part of a larger downshift in refinancing from last year’s 
fast clip.

As a share of total issuance, the second quarter’s 66% 
weighting to refinancing was consistent with the first quarter, 
both well below last year’s marks of 82% in the second 
quarter and 71% in the first quarter.
For gross issuance totals, incremental debt — for more 
ambitious fiscal priorities, such as M&A/LBO funding 
or dividend payouts — has provided an offset to lower 
refinancing, but even there the totals are cooler than most 
had expected heading into the summer months. 
Led by more than $20 billion printed by non-sponsored 
companies, bond issuance for M&A and LBO funds was at a 
four-year high of $27 billion to June 17. 
M&A deals cleared for Acrisure, New Home, Ryman 
Hospitality Properties, Herc Holdings, Shift4Pay, QXO, 
Excelerate Energy and Owens and Minor. (Among those, 
only New Home is sponsored.)
Meantime, bond funding for LBOs was sparse under the 
tariff shadow. 
There were late-month pitches for Skechers and Sizzling 
Platter in June, but those were the first LBO bonds on offer 
since Everi/IGT (May 8), which itself was the first LBO deal 
since March.
LBOs are running at about 3% of this year’s volume, same 
as last year and right around the level in pandemic-era 
2020 (2.9%). 
Under a Trump administration, desks were banking on a 
vigorous showing in LBOs this year, but that’s a thready 
pulse: full-year shares were from 6-15% from 2021-2023, 
and the annual average was above 5% from 2010-2019, 
according to LCD.

So far, there are no signs of issuers rushing headlong to erect 
liquidity bridges, as they did in 2020 when lockdowns choked 
off cash flows. Deals broadly earmarked for GCP are about 8% 
of YTD issuance, double last year’s low share, but less than 
half of 2020’s 17%-plus.   
Senior class
One area of concern is the clear skew to higher-quality issuers 
in this year’s mix. Some 42% of all bonds have been double-B 
rated at issuance this year, an all-time high. Meantime, deals 
rated CCC or lower were 2% of volume, half of last year’s rate 
and in line with 2023’s historic low. As top-tier borrowers 
play an outsized role, senior unsecured issuance is running at 
about 60% of total issuance, up from 56% for all of last year. 
This is a trend towards “normalcy,” as senior issuance was 67-
69% from 2019-2022, and 70-80% from 2011-2018.

While the current macroeconomic outlook arguably is 
bleaker — or at least as uncertain — than under than that 
trailing inflation threat, funding conditions remain remarkably 
accommodative, the April downturn notwithstanding. 
Since April — when issuers paid T+425 on average to clear 
new unsecured HY deals, a 15-month high — clearing spreads 
narrowed to T+277 in May (58 bps tighter year to year) and 
T+316 in early June (about unchanged year to year).
Meantime, monthly unsecured yields at pricing (including a 
low at 7% in March and a high at 8.13% in April) have been 
below year-ago levels in all six months so far in 2025. 
Four of the six tranches priced this year with sub-6% reoffer 
yields priced in May, via double-B borrowers Carnival 
Cruises, Teva Pharmaceutical, Crown Holdings and Seagate 
Data Storage.

Keep it short(ish)
Resilient costs are allowing issuers to stretch their maturities, 
if gradually. The share of deals dated five years or less has 
subsided to 36% this year, from 40% last year and an all-time 
high of 45% in 2023. Issuers narrowed their funding horizons 
during the lockdowns as well (that share was 44% in 2020).
On an historical basis, though, this ongoing concentration 
of shorter terms remains unusual, and it perhaps adds to 
refinancing risks down the road. From 2010 to 2019 (and also 
in 2021), the share of deals dated five years or shorter never 
exceeded 30%, and it averaged 21% during those years.

US HIGH-YIELD BOND WEEKLY WRAP
June 26, 2025
Cash-bond prices advanced over 
the week and the new-issue pipeline 
churned as a roiling geopolitical 
backdrop failed to diminish risk 
appetite. Treasury rates eased further 
off their June peaks, while spreads 
edged five basis points tighter from 
Monday’s open, to 293 bps off the 
curve, well below the three-month 
average of T+332. Meanwhile, the 
option-adjusted spread on LCD’s 
flow-name sample of liquid high-yield 
issues tightened 19 bps this week, to 
T+282, and the average bid rose 102 
bps, to 95.18% of par, as 13 of the 15 
constituent issues traded higher.
Gray Media’s 5.375% senior notes due 
2031 logged the most significant gains 
in the flow-name sample, adding 4.25 
points to trade around 15 points above 
their early-May levels, at 74.5 for a 
yield of roughly 11.04%. That’s as the 
company continues to draft optimism 
surrounding the deregulation of the 
broadcasting industry. 
Against those gains, there was 
one unchanged level, for Tenet 
Healthcare’s issue, and one decliner, 
Transocean’s 8.75% senior 2030 
bonds. The latter pared intraweek 
losses to 0.75 points as oil prices 
recovered from a sharp slide early this 
week and were changing hands in a 
102.75 context for a 4.45% yield.
Another notable energy-sector decliner 
was Vital Energy’s (NYSE: VTLE) 
March print of 7.875% eight-year senior 
bonds, which tumbled 2.25 points 
to an 85 context and an 11.06% yield 
after touching a nine-week high of 92 
on June 13. Raymond James analysts 
downgraded Vital Energy’s stock to 
Underperform, from Outperform, citing 
the company’s relatively high 1.9x 
leverage ratio and its lower inventory 
life in the Permian Basin.
High-yield secondary market: Chasing the sun
The energy picture also weighed on 
Crescent Energy Finance’s Monday 
offering of 8.375% 8.5-year senior 
notes, knocking the bonds down to low 
trades at 99.25, from 100.375/100.75 
on the break. Meanwhile, a par-
priced $650 million offering of 9.125% 
five-year senior notes (BB-/B3/BB-) 
for Tidewater Inc., which provides 
offshore support services, probed 103 
on the highs even after pricing through 
guidance in the 9.50-9.75% range.
The week’s smorgasbord of new 
prints included tightly priced M&A 
offerings from Sizzling Platter (9.5% 
seven-year senior secured notes) and 
StoneX Group (6.875% second-lien 
senior secured notes), which traded 
up at 102.25 and 101.25, respectively. 
The trend toward cross-border deals 
was represented by Czechoslovak 
Group’s $1 billion print of senior 
secured 5.5-year notes, priced through 
initial whispers in the 6.75% to yield 
6.5%. Proceeds, along with those of 
a concurrent €1 billion placement 
of 5.25% notes also due 2031, are 
earmarked to refinance €717 million 
of dollar-denominated FRNs that the 
issuer priced in December at S+700. 
The dollar bonds were quoted in a 
101.1/101.35 context, according to 
MarketAxess.
Azorra Aviation Holdings’ $550 
million placement of 7.75% 5.5-year 
senior notes was trading on the highs 
on Thursday, at 101.5, while Delek 
Logistics Partners’ $700 million print 
of 7.375% eight-year senior notes was 
hovering around par re-offer after 
topping out at 100.75. On the other 
hand, Lendmark Financial Services’ 
tender-backing offering of 8.75% 
five-year senior notes was lingering 
on the lows, at 98.75, after pricing 
at an OID of 98.989 to yield 9%. Top 
trades for those notes, which had been 
guided for a yield in the 8.75-9% range, 
came at 99.5.

US HIGH-YIELD BOND WEEKLY WRAP
June 26, 2025
Remarkably consistent deal flow in 
June included a roughly $32 billion 
influx June 23-26, which blasted past 
subdued expectations for about $20-25 
billion for the entire week. Issuance 
is $96 billion for June, and a Monday 
issuance window on June 30 will 
close out a turbulent, but ultimately 
productive, quarter.
After May’s dramatics (there were six 
double-digit session totals last month, 
including a $25 billion session on May 
6), June’s totals are more regulated. 
No session has topped $10 billion, and 
the average session produced $6.8 
billion ($7.9 billion this week), from $8.8 
billion in May.
Still, June’s is a strong showing given 
the strength of the headwinds buffeting 
global markets. Last year, issuance was 
similar at $97 billion all month, up from 
$89 billion in June 2023 and $69 billion 
in June 2022. 
Issuance for this year ($852 billion) is 
about 2% ahead of last year’s hot pace. 
(These totals trail only the $1.14 trillion 
printed through June 2020 as the Fed 
High-grade market: On the regular
played lender of last resort during the 
pandemic.)
All of this week’s supply backed 
refinancing or general corporate needs. 
Those fundings are the driving force for 
this year’s strong pace, as acquisition-
driven deal flows disappoint to the 
downside under what was expected to 
be a supportive regime in Washington. 
M&A issuance held at $36 billion for the 
quarter, half the first-quarter amount 
($73 billion) and about $5 billion less 
than the total in Q2 2024. YTD M&A 
volume ($109 billion) is 13% less 
year to year and just 6% ahead of the 
2023 pace.
As for trailing efforts, the EU put Mars 
Inc.’s $43 billion play for snacks giant 
Kellanova under intense scrutiny 
for potential consumer impact. Mars 
priced $26 billion of bonds to back the 
deal, and that harsh spotlight stopped 
a tightening move in its tracks. The $5 
billion tranche of 5.20% 2035 notes, 
which traded at all-time tights at T+76 
mid-month, backed up to T+83-84 this 
week. (That’s still firm versus a T+95 
reoffer spread at pricing on March 5.)  
Meantime, a relative hot streak for 
IG corporate performance — in a 
previously chilly year for performance 
broadly — includes a 1.3% gain June 
1-25 (per the Morningstar index), 
keeping pace with HY this month and 
narrowing the YTD gap to half a point. 
(To June 25, HY is up 4.1% and IG is up 
3.6%, per Morningstar.) 
Trading in bank bellwethers is indicative 
of this positive trajectory. One of the 
week’s most active issues — Bank of 
America’s 5.464% senior notes due 
2036 — traded Thursday at 102% of par 
to yield 5.20%, or T+93. That spread 
matches the all-time tightest trade 
recorded earlier this month, and it was 
sharply tighter from pricing (at par) at 
T+115 on May 6.
As for tariff bellwethers, Ford Motor 
Credit 6.50% 2035 notes — priced 
early January at T+193 — linger wide of 
pricing (trades were T+235 Thursday) 
and just shy of par. Still, that’s a marked 
improvement since the notes touched 
T+312 (95% of par) in early April post 
the initial April 2 tariff shocks. 
— John Atkins

US HIGH-YIELD BOND WEEKLY WRAP
June 26, 2025
As the second quarter of 2025 winds down, a wave of credit 
downgrades and restructuring moves has underscored 
deepening financial stress across sectors, with May marking 
the highest monthly global default count in nearly five years, 
according to S&P Global Ratings.
The global corporate default count hit 19 in May, the highest 
monthly tally since October 2020, according to S&P Global 
Ratings. The year-to-date default count stands at 53 as of 
May 31, below the 69 defaults at the same point in 2024, the 
agency said.
Regionally, the US led May’s default count with nine, bringing 
its YTD total to 30, while Europe saw six defaults in May, for a 
YTD tally of 16, S&P noted.
In corporate news, automobile chip maker Wolfspeed 
Inc. inked a restructuring support agreement (RSA) with 
stakeholders to restructure its balance sheet and cut debt by 
around $4.6 billion via a Chapter 11 bankruptcy filing that is 
expected to take place by July 1.
Transactions outlined in the RSA include holders of senior 
secured notes exchanging into new notes, with $250 million of 
the secured notes redeemed at 109.875; holders of $5.2 billion 
of convertible notes and Renesas’ existing loan exchanging 
into $500 million of new second-lien notes plus 95% of the 
new common stock; and current equity holders converting 
into 3% or 5% of the new common stock (depending on 
certain regulatory approvals).
In addition, Wolfspeed will issue $275 million of new second-
lien convertible notes in a transaction backstopped by certain 
current convertible noteholders.
In ratings activity, S&P downgraded rehabilitation and 
physical therapy company Upstream Newco Inc., dba 
Upstream Rehabilitation, to CCC, from CCC+, citing 
weakening liquidity. Upstream’s first-lien term loan and 
revolver were also cut to CCC, from CCC+, while its second-
lien term loan was lowered to CC, from CCC-.
Upstream’s 2024 revenue grew 1%, versus S&P projections for 
5% growth, while EBITDA margins narrowed, with a resultant 
decline in liquidity, the agency said. S&P has lowered its 2025 
projections, forecasting leverage of roughly 16.3x this year.
Moody’s downgraded Liberty Communications PR Holding 
LP and LCPR Senior Secured Financing DAC’s senior secured 
rating and LCPR Loan Financing LLC’s term loan to Caa1, from 
B3, saying it views Liberty PR’s liquidity as “weak.”
Distressed market: Out of sync
Moody’s expects the issuer to struggle because of its limited 
scale, operating in two markets, the US Virgin Islands and 
Puerto Rico, which are relatively small and competitive. 
S&P downgraded medical imaging company Carestream 
Health Inc. to CCC+, from B-, citing declining revenue and 
cash flow. S&P also downgraded the company’s senior 
secured rating to CCC+, from B-. 
S&P said Carestream’s revenue fell $53 million in 2025’s 
first quarter, on the heels of a $25 million decline in revenue 
in 2024’s fourth quarter, with the decline attributed to 
customers transitioning to digital medical records, especially 
in China. Carestream’s digital radiography business is also 
experiencing sales declines, S&P said.
Moody’s downgraded automotive supplier Burgess Point 
Purchaser Corporation, dba Terrepower and fka BBB 
Industries, to Caa2, from B3, citing the company’s “weak” 
liquidity. The agency also lowered Terrepower’s senior 
secured bank debt to Caa1, from B2.
In 2025, Terrepower may grow revenue following its 
acquisition of All Star Auto Lights in August 2024 and expand 
EBITDA margins on cost cuts, Moody’s said, adding that 
Terrepower may also continue to generate negative free 
cash flow.
S&P downgraded natural food ingredient supplier FFP 
Holdings Group Inc., dba Florida Food Products, to CCC-
, from CCC, citing rising default risk because of cash flow 
deficits. S&P also lowered Florida Food’s first-lien debt to 
CCC-, from CCC, and its second-lien term loan to C, from CC.

declined.  As a result, the agency

S&P downgraded plastics distributor 
GPD Companies Inc., fka Nexeo 
Plastics, to Selective Default, or SD, 
from CC, citing a completed exchange 
offer of its 10.125% senior unsecured 
notes due 2026 for cash plus new 12.5% 
senior secured notes due 2029.
S&P said it considered the par-for-par 
transaction to be “distressed” because 
noteholders weren’t adequately 
compensated for the extended 
maturity. 
Moody’s also weighed in on GPD after 
the debt swap, affirming its Caa1 rating. 
The agency also revised GPD’s outlook 
to positive, from stable, assigned a 
Caa2 rating to the new 12.5.% notes 
and temporarily appended a limited 
default designation to the company’s 
probability of default rating (PDR), 
revising it to Caa1-PD/LD.
Moody’s noted that GPD reduced 
roughly $175 million of the notes’ 
outstanding balance by applying 
Distrupol sale proceeds, while a $40 
million equity injection by sponsor 
One Rock Capital Partners was used 
to partially fund the exchange’s cash 
component.
Away from downgrades, Moody’s and 
S&P both chimed in on pet food maker 
Woof Holdings LLC, dba Wellness Pet, 
after a balance sheet restructuring.
Moody’s affirmed Wellness Pet at 
Caa3, and revised its outlook to 
stable, from negative. The agency also 
temporarily appended a limited default 
designation to Woof’s PDR, revising it to 
Caa3-PD/LD.
Wellness Pet put in place a new 
$100 million first-lien first-out loan 
while existing first-lien and second-
lien lenders, as well as sponsor 
Clearlake, swapped into new debt. 
Moody’s believes that following the 
restructuring, Wellness Pet continues 
to carry “unsustainably high” leverage, 
while it runs negative free cash flow 
and faces challenges in completing an 
operational turnaround.
S&P, meanwhile, upgraded Wellness 
Pet to CCC+, from SD, citing the 
company’s improved liquidity after the 
restructuring. S&P said management 
has “outlined various initiatives” 
to reduce revenue declines and 
improve margins.
S&P upgraded photo printing company 
Photo Holdings LLC, dba Shutterfly, 
to B-, from CCC+, citing improved 
credit metrics. S&P also upgraded 
the company’s secured ratings by 
one notch.
S&P projects that Shutterfly will 
show no revenue growth this year, 
but gain around 3% in 2026, along 
with margin improvements leading 
to higher EBITDA in 2025. The agency 
also said the company’s free operating 
cash flow (FOCF) covered all interest 
expense in 2024, and that the agency 
expects positive FOCF this year and in 
2026 as well.
S&P upgraded tape and film maker Iris 
Holdings Inc, dba IPG and also known as 
Intertape Polymer Group, to B-, from 
CCC+, citing improving profitability. 
S&P also upgraded the company’s 
secured term loan to B-, from CCC+, 
and the senior unsecured notes to CCC, 
from CCC-.
S&P projects EBITDA margin 
improvement despite a “slower demand 
environment” because of lower 
raw material costs and productivity 
improvements. The agency also 
foresees annual low-to-mid-single-digit 
percentage gains in revenue after 2025 
and “modest deleveraging” over the 
next few years.
